title: KQL Projected Columns
scenario: You are reviewing DeviceProcessEvents and need only the device name, process name, and timestamp for the last day.
question: Which KQL pattern returns only those fields?

options.text: DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(1d) | project DeviceName, FileName, Timestamp
options.explanation: where limits the time range and project returns only the requested columns.

options.text: DeviceProcessEvents | select DeviceName, FileName, Timestamp | time 1d
options.explanation: select and time are not the KQL operators used for this task.

options.text: DeviceProcessEvents | summarize DeviceName, FileName, Timestamp
options.explanation: summarize requires aggregation expressions and is not a column-selection operator.

options.text: DeviceProcessEvents | extend DeviceName, FileName, Timestamp
options.explanation: extend creates calculated columns; it does not select existing columns or filter time.

title: KQL Aggregation by User
scenario: You need a count of failed sign-ins grouped by UserPrincipalName and want only users with more than 10 failures.
question: Which query structure is correct?

options.text: SigninLogs | where ResultType != 0 | project UserPrincipalName | where count > 10
options.explanation: After project there is no count column, and count must be calculated before it can be filtered.

options.text: SigninLogs | where ResultType != 0 | summarize Failures=count() by UserPrincipalName | where Failures > 10
options.explanation: summarize creates the per-user count, and the following where applies the threshold.

options.text: SigninLogs | count UserPrincipalName > 10
options.explanation: count is an aggregation function used inside summarize, not a standalone filter command.

options.text: SigninLogs | distinct UserPrincipalName | limit 10
options.explanation: distinct removes duplicates but does not count failures or apply a threshold.

title: KQL Joining Identity and Process Data
scenario: You want to correlate a suspicious process with the user who was logged on to the same device.
question: Which KQL capability is most appropriate when the events are in separate tables?

options.text: union only
options.explanation: union combines rows with a similar shape; it does not match related rows by device or time.

options.text: project-away only
options.explanation: project-away removes columns and cannot correlate records.

options.text: join using shared entity fields such as DeviceId
options.explanation: join correlates rows from different tables using a common key, such as DeviceId, with optional time constraints.

options.text: render timechart
options.explanation: render changes presentation and does not create relationships between tables.

title: KQL Parsing URL Data
scenario: A custom log contains a Url field. You need to extract the host and find requests to a suspicious domain.
question: Which function is designed to parse a URL into components?

options.text: parse_url()
options.explanation: parse_url returns URL components such as the host, path, and scheme for further filtering.

options.text: count()
options.explanation: count aggregates rows and does not decompose URL text.

options.text: bin()
options.explanation: bin rounds values into time or numeric bins and does not parse URLs.

options.text: arg_max()
options.explanation: arg_max selects a row with a maximum value and does not parse URL components.

title: KQL Timechart
scenario: You need to visualize failed sign-in volume in 15-minute intervals over the last six hours.
question: Which query design produces the required time series?

options.text: where TimeGenerated > ago(6h) | summarize count()
options.explanation: This creates one total and does not group results into time intervals.

options.text: where TimeGenerated > ago(6h) | summarize Failures=count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 15m) | render timechart
options.explanation: bin creates 15-minute buckets and render timechart displays the resulting series.

options.text: sort by TimeGenerated | render piechart
options.explanation: Sorting and a pie chart do not create time buckets.

options.text: distinct TimeGenerated | render timechart
options.explanation: distinct removes duplicate timestamps but does not count failures.

title: Windows Security Events via AMA
scenario: You need selected Windows security events from Azure VMs and want to control collection by event set.
question: Which implementation is appropriate?

options.text: Install AMA and associate a DCR that selects the required Windows Security event set
options.explanation: AMA collects the events and the DCR defines the machines and event selection.

options.text: Install a workbook on every VM
options.explanation: Workbooks visualize data and do not collect Windows events.

options.text: Use a Sentinel watchlist as the event source
options.explanation: Watchlists contain reference data and do not collect operating-system events.

options.text: Use an analytics rule to ingest events
options.explanation: Analytics rules detect ingested data; they are not collection agents.

title: Windows Event Forwarding
scenario: A domain has many on-premises Windows servers and you want to collect events through a Windows Event Collector rather than install an agent on every server.
question: Which design matches Windows Event Forwarding?

options.text: Forward events from source computers to a collector, then collect the forwarded events into Sentinel
options.explanation: WEF centralizes Windows event forwarding at a collector before Sentinel ingestion.

options.text: Send every event directly to a workbook
options.explanation: Workbooks do not receive Windows events and cannot replace WEF or a collector.

options.text: Put the server names in a watchlist
options.explanation: A watchlist does not transport event records.

options.text: Use a KQL job as the Windows agent
options.explanation: KQL jobs query retained data and are not collection agents.

title: CEF via AMA Architecture
scenario: A network appliance sends Common Event Format messages to a Linux log forwarder.
question: What must be configured for Sentinel ingestion?

options.text: AMA on the Linux forwarder, the CEF connector, and a DCR associated with the forwarder
options.explanation: CEF via AMA uses the Linux forwarder, connector, and DCR to define collection and routing.

options.text: AMA on the appliance only, with no connector
options.explanation: The appliance is not the collection endpoint in this design, and the connector is still required.

options.text: An Entra connector on the forwarder
options.explanation: Entra collection is unrelated to CEF messages from a network appliance.

options.text: A workbook and a scheduled query
options.explanation: These operate after ingestion and cannot receive CEF by themselves.

title: Azure Resource Diagnostic Settings
scenario: You need resource logs from an Azure Key Vault in a Sentinel workspace.
question: Which configuration sends the resource logs to Sentinel?

options.text: Configure the Key Vault diagnostic setting to send the required categories to the Log Analytics workspace
options.explanation: Resource diagnostic settings route supported resource logs to the selected Log Analytics workspace.

options.text: Install AMA inside the Key Vault
options.explanation: Managed services such as Key Vault do not accept an operating-system agent installation.

options.text: Create a user watchlist with vault names
options.explanation: A watchlist does not collect Key Vault resource logs.

options.text: Create a Defender XDR device group
options.explanation: Device groups manage endpoint scope and are unrelated to Key Vault diagnostics.

title: Threat Intelligence Indicator Ingestion
scenario: Your threat intelligence provider supplies STIX/TAXII indicators and the SOC wants detections when those indicators match events.
question: Which data path should you use?

options.text: Threat intelligence connector into ThreatIntelligenceIndicator, then a matching analytics or hunting query
options.explanation: The connector ingests indicators into the threat-intelligence table, which queries can correlate with event data.

options.text: Store the feed as a workbook layout
options.explanation: A workbook is presentation content and does not ingest or normalize indicators.

options.text: Put the feed in a Windows event channel
options.explanation: Windows event channels are not the appropriate storage or ingestion path for STIX/TAXII indicators.

options.text: Create an incident for every indicator before ingestion
options.explanation: Indicators should be ingested and correlated; creating an incident for each one creates noise.

title: Search Job Result Table
scenario: A search job scans a large historical dataset for a hash. You need to investigate the matches repeatedly afterward.
question: What should you do with the result?

options.text: Use the generated search-result table as the focused source for follow-up KQL investigation
options.explanation: Search jobs make broad historical matches available in a result table that can be queried for detailed analysis.

options.text: Assume the search result is already a confirmed incident
options.explanation: A match is evidence to validate, not automatically a confirmed incident.

options.text: Delete the original tables
options.explanation: Search results do not replace source retention and deleting evidence is unsafe.

options.text: Convert the result to a workbook without reviewing records
options.explanation: Visualization before validation does not establish whether the matches are malicious.

title: Summary Rule Use
scenario: A high-volume table must support repeated dashboards that need hourly counts, while raw events are not needed for every dashboard refresh.
question: Which Sentinel capability is designed for this repeated aggregation?

options.text: A summary rule that periodically aggregates data into a queryable summary table
options.explanation: Summary rules precompute recurring aggregates so dashboards can query smaller, purpose-built results.

options.text: A one-time search job for every dashboard load
options.explanation: Repeated search jobs are inefficient for a recurring aggregation workload.

options.text: A device isolation action
options.explanation: Device isolation is response containment and has no aggregation role.

options.text: A watchlist of hourly totals maintained manually
options.explanation: Manual watchlists are not a reliable automated aggregation mechanism.

title: Hunting Query Bookmarks
scenario: An analyst finds suspicious records during a hunt and wants to preserve the evidence with entities and notes for the investigation.
question: What should the analyst use?

options.text: A hunting bookmark linked to the investigation
options.explanation: Bookmarks preserve selected hunting results and context so the analyst can use them during investigation.

options.text: A retention-tier change
options.explanation: Changing retention does not preserve the analyst's selected evidence or notes.

options.text: A connector restart
options.explanation: Restarting collection does not preserve findings.

options.text: A password reset for the analyst
options.explanation: A password reset is unrelated to recording hunting evidence.

title: NRT Analytics Rule
scenario: A detection must run with very low latency on a supported table and does not require a multi-table join.
question: Which analytics rule type should you evaluate?

options.text: A monthly workbook
options.explanation: A workbook is reporting content and is not a low-latency detection rule.

options.text: A near-real-time analytics rule
options.explanation: NRT rules are designed for low-latency detection on supported scenarios and tables.

options.text: A watchlist upload
options.explanation: A watchlist stores reference data and does not generate detections.

options.text: A manual notebook export
options.explanation: Manual exports cannot provide continuous low-latency alerting.

title: Connector Validation Query
scenario: You configured Windows Security Events via AMA and need to validate ingestion before enabling a detection.
question: Which query is the best first validation?

options.text: SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h) | summarize count() by Computer
options.explanation: This checks recent records and shows which computers are actually sending events.

options.text: SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(1y) | render piechart
options.explanation: A year-wide visualization is unnecessarily broad and does not directly validate current source coverage.

options.text: Heartbeat | summarize count()
options.explanation: Heartbeat confirms agent presence but does not prove Windows Security events reached SecurityEvent.

options.text: SigninLogs | count
options.explanation: Sign-in logs validate an identity connector, not Windows Security Events via AMA.

title: Custom Log Ingestion
scenario: A SaaS vendor provides JSON events through an API and has no built-in Sentinel connector. You need a supported ingestion design.
question: Which approach should you evaluate?

options.text: Use the Logs Ingestion API with a DCR and a custom table, or a supported custom connector pattern
options.explanation: The API and DCR provide a controlled schema and ingestion path for sources without a built-in connector.

options.text: Paste JSON into a workbook
options.explanation: Workbooks cannot serve as a durable ingestion pipeline.

options.text: Rename the JSON file to .evtx
options.explanation: Changing a file extension does not convert an API payload into Windows event data.

options.text: Create an empty analytics rule
options.explanation: A detection rule cannot collect vendor data.

title: Connector Data Collection Scope
scenario: Only production servers should send Windows security events to the workspace; development servers must be excluded.
question: Where should you express this machine scope?

options.text: In the DCR association or resource scope used by the connector
options.explanation: DCR associations determine which resources receive the collection configuration.

options.text: In the incident title
options.explanation: An incident title cannot control data collection.

options.text: In a workbook color setting
options.explanation: Presentation settings do not control the source machines.

options.text: In the KQL render command
options.explanation: Rendering affects output display, not which machines send telemetry.

title: KQL Empty Results Diagnosis
scenario: A KQL query returns no rows even though the connector dashboard says Connected.
question: What should you check first?

options.text: Time range, table name, workspace, and whether the expected source has recently ingested records
options.explanation: An empty result can come from an incorrect time range or table as well as a collection problem; these checks separate query and ingestion causes.

options.text: Change the portal theme
options.explanation: Portal appearance does not affect query results.

options.text: Delete the connector
options.explanation: Deleting the connector destroys configuration before the cause is understood.

options.text: Create a second identical rule
options.explanation: Duplicating a rule does not fix a query or ingestion issue.

title: Notebook Hunting Workflow
scenario: A hunter wants a repeatable notebook that retrieves data, transforms it, records findings, and can be rerun by another analyst.
question: Which practice best supports this workflow?

options.text: Use the Sentinel MCP Server or approved notebook connection, parameterize time and entities, and record query outputs
options.explanation: A reusable notebook needs an approved connection, explicit parameters, and preserved outputs so another analyst can reproduce the hunt.

options.text: Copy screenshots from the portal into the notebook
options.explanation: Screenshots are not reproducible data or executable hunting steps.

options.text: Hard-code a personal token in every cell
options.explanation: Personal embedded secrets are unsafe and make the notebook difficult to transfer.

options.text: Delete the notebook after exporting a PDF
options.explanation: Deleting the executable workflow removes reproducibility.

title: KQL Materialized Aggregation
scenario: A query repeatedly computes the same high-volume aggregation and interactive performance is poor.
question: Which improvement should you consider?

options.text: Use a summary rule or other pre-aggregation strategy when the workload is recurring
options.explanation: Pre-aggregating recurring results reduces the amount of raw data scanned for each query.

options.text: Add more columns with project-away
options.explanation: Removing columns can reduce payload but does not solve a recurring high-volume aggregation by itself.

options.text: Run the same query more often
options.explanation: More frequent raw scans increase work and do not improve performance.

options.text: Move the query into a watchlist
options.explanation: Watchlists store reference values and cannot execute aggregations.
